summary: Arabic marks a definite noun with the prefix al- (الْ) and an indefinite noun with nunation (tanwīn).

askYourself: Is the noun specific or generic (→ al-) or one of many (→ tanwīn)?
Did I drop the tanwīn after adding al-?

traps: Generic statements use al-: هِيَ تَأْكُلُ الْخِيَارَ = she eats cucumbers (in general).

notes.text: English the and a become a prefix and an ending: الْبَيْتُ (the house), بَيْتٌ (a house). The fossil al- lives on in English words taken from Arabic: alcohol, algebra, alchemy.

Spanish loans keep the Arabic article — with the sun-letter assimilation: aceite (الزَّيْت az-zayt), azúcar (السُّكَّر as-sukkar), arroz (الرُّزّ ar-ruzz, a variant of أَرُزّ). Spanish has un / una for “a”; Arabic uses the ending -un.
French le / la and un / une become a prefix and an ending: الْبَيْتُ / بَيْتٌ. There is no partitive du / de la: أُرِيدُ قَهْوَةً is “I want (some) coffee”.
Greek has ο / η / το and ένας / μία / ένα; Arabic has one prefix for “the” (الْ, the same for every gender, number and case) and no separate “a”: the ending -un says it.
Russian has no articles; Arabic marks every noun: الْبَيْتُ (the house) or بَيْتٌ (a house). Ask: do we both know which one? Then الْ.
Hindi has no articles (एक means “one”); Arabic marks every noun as definite (الْ) or indefinite (-un).
Persian marks “a” with an ending too (کتابی, a book) but has no “the” — only -rā on a definite object; Arabic puts الْ on every definite noun.
Marathi has no articles; Arabic marks every noun as definite or indefinite.
Turkish has bir for “a” and no “the” — only the -ı of a definite object; Arabic puts الْ on every definite noun, subject or object.
Japanese has no articles; Arabic marks every noun: الْبَيْتُ or بَيْتٌ.
Finnish has no articles; Arabic marks every noun, and a noun meant in general takes الْ: أُحِبُّ الْقَهْوَةَ (I like coffee).
Hungarian has a / az and egy and uses the article for things in general too (szeretem a kávét); Arabic does this with الْ, and says “a” with the ending -un.
Swahili has no articles; Arabic marks every noun as definite (الْ) or indefinite (-un).
Luganda has no articles; Arabic marks every noun as definite (الْ) or indefinite (-un).
Vietnamese has no articles (một means “one”); Arabic marks every noun: الْبَيْتُ or بَيْتٌ.
Inuktitut has no articles; Arabic marks every noun as definite (الْ) or indefinite (-un).
